title: Salvation came to this house (Luke 19:1–10)
hook: Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and repays four times over

segments.voice: Yesterday, a blind man shouted louder, and Jesus stood still and asked, what do you want? Who did you stop for? Day five hundred sixty-eight.

Still in Jericho. You probably know the first half of this story: a short, rich chief tax collector named Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore tree to see over the crowd, and Jesus stops underneath and calls him by name. "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Today we follow them inside. Because what Zacchaeus says at his own table, with the whole town grumbling outside, is one of the most surprising speeches in the Gospels. Nobody asks him for it. Jesus doesn't preach. Zacchaeus just stands up.
screen: `TODAY I MUST ABIDE AT THY HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First the grumbling. Luke says they all murmured, "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." Tax collectors worked for Rome and often took more than they were owed, and a chief tax collector got rich on it. Then Zacchaeus stands and says, in the King James Bible: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Half to the poor. And fourfold back to anyone he cheated. Here's why fourfold is striking. The law of Moses had rules for paying back what you'd taken. For many wrongs, you returned it and added a fifth. But for a stolen sheep, Exodus says: "he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep." Zacchaeus reaches for the steepest standard, as if he'd stolen sheep from every one of them. And nobody told him to. Jesus never mentioned money. Being welcomed did what lectures hadn't. A few scholars point out that the Greek verbs are present tense, I give, I restore, and wonder if he's describing what he already does. Most read it as a new promise, there and then. Then Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham." This day. Today is one of Luke's favorite words. The angels used it at his birth: born this day. Jesus used it in Nazareth: this day, this scripture is fulfilled. And on the cross, he'll say today again. Salvation in Luke isn't only someday. It walks into a house, sits down to dinner, and changes how the money moves.
screen: then, large: `THIS DAY IS SALVATION COME TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repay someone generously. Settle and breathe. Think back. Is there anyone you owe something to? Money you borrowed and forgot, a favor never returned, credit you took that was really theirs, time you took from someone without giving back. Don't spiral into guilt. Just pick one. Now imagine paying it back, not exactly, but generously, more than you owe, the way Zacchaeus did. What would that look like? A check, a thank-you, a public word giving them the credit. If you pray, you can give thanks for being welcomed first. The bell holds the time.
Salvation came to this house. Welcomed before he changed, Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and repays fourfold, and Jesus says: this day, salvation.
screen: `SALVATION CAME TO THIS HOUSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: today, salvation. Today, pay back the one thing you thought of, and add a little extra. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians often read Zacchaeus when talking about repentance that changes behavior; in many churches, especially Catholic and Orthodox, making restitution is part of turning back after a wrong, and the story is read at the dedication of churches.

original.note: Greek: today, this day. one of Luke's favorite words, from the angels' song to the cross.

trapdoor: what you thought: a short man climbs a tree.
what it means: welcomed before he changed, Zacchaeus changes how his money moves, and salvation arrives today, in his house.
what a scholar hears: fourfold is the Exodus penalty for a stolen sheep, the present-tense verbs are debated, and today threads through Luke from the birth to the cross.

notes: Year one (day 59, 'he knows your name') told the tree-climbing; this day centers the restitution and 'today'.
Restitution laws: add a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7); fourfold for a sheep (Exodus 22:1). Confirm.
Present-tense debate (δίδωμι, ἀποδίδωμι in 19:8): minority 'customary' reading presented as 'a few scholars'. Confirm.
Luke 2:11 and 4:21 are alluded to without quotation ('born this day', 'this day, this scripture is fulfilled').
Dedication-of-a-church reading (Luke 19:1–10): traditional in the Roman Rite. Confirm.
